explanations.explanation: Matthew tells us up front that these are Sadducees “…who say there is no resurrection…” (Matthew 22:23). So before they say a word, we already know where their question is headed. It's like a friend asking for advice when he's already made up his mind. You nailed it, baker.

Matthew says the opposite. He describes the Sadducees as those “…who say there is no resurrection…” (Matthew 22:23). He tells us that before they ask anything. So when that question comes, we know what they believe.

explanations.answer: To raise up children for his brother
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The Sadducees say Moses declared the brother is to marry the widow and raise up offspring for the man who died. The point is children for the brother who had none. Short, simple and right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: To pay off his brother's debts
explanations.explanation: Close to a bill collector's dream, but no. The Sadducees mention nothing about debts. They say the brother marries the widow to raise up offspring for the one who died without children. I've seen some hard bills in my day, friend, but this one isn't about money.

explanations.answer: To look after his brother's flocks
explanations.explanation: Flocks never come up, friend. The Sadducees say the brother marries the widow to raise up offspring for the man who died. This is about children, not sheep. Nobody needs a brother-in-law with a shepherd's staff in this verse.

Right on the money. The Sadducees say the first brother married, died without children, and left his wife to his brother. That matches the rule they just quoted from Moses. And it sets the table for the rest of their story.

Not his father, friend. The Sadducees say the first brother left his wife to his brother. That fits the rule they brought up from Moses, where a brother is the one who steps in. A father never enters their story.

No servant in this story, baker. The Sadducees say the first brother left his wife to his brother. That's the same brother rule they quoted from Moses. Nobody in their tale gets handed off to hired help.

explanations.answer: Which brother will be her husband
explanations.explanation: That's their question, baker. They ask, “In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven?” and add that all of them were married to her (Matthew 22:28). They've lined up seven brothers like dominoes and want Jesus to pick one. Notice the question is built on the idea that she would be married to one of them in the resurrection.

explanations.answer: Which brother she loved the most
explanations.explanation: Love never comes up, friend. The Sadducees ask, “…whose wife will she be of the seven?” (Matthew 22:28). They want to know whose wife she will be, and the text gives no word about who she loved. I'd be curious about that one too, but they never ask it.

explanations.answer: Which brother will inherit her land
explanations.explanation: No land in this question, baker. They ask, “…whose wife will she be of the seven?” (Matthew 22:28). It's about whose wife she will be, with all seven brothers in the mix. Nobody in their story brings up a deed or a property line.

explanations.answer: They don't know the Scriptures or God's power
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus says, “You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.” (Matthew 22:29). Two things are named, the Scriptures and God's power. He says it straight, and then He gets to work answering them.

explanations.answer: They spoke without asking the priests first
explanations.explanation: Jesus never says anything about asking the priests. His reason is this: “You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.” (Matthew 22:29). He puts the problem on what they don't know. That's the whole reason He gives.

explanations.answer: They brought their question on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: The Sabbath isn't in this conversation, friend. Jesus says, “You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.” (Matthew 22:29). He names the Scriptures and God's power. No calendar involved.

Jesus says the opposite, friend. He says, “In the resurrection, people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven.” (Matthew 22:30). So the seven-brothers puzzle runs into what the resurrection is really like. Keep that verse handy.

Yes, baker. Jesus says people will neither marry nor be given in marriage in the resurrection, and that they will be like the angels in heaven (Matthew 22:30). The Sadducees built their whole puzzle on marriage carrying on. Jesus answers that puzzle in one line.
That's the one, baker. Jesus asks, “…have you not read what God said to you…” (Matthew 22:31). He points them to God's own words. And then He quotes them.

explanations.answer: What the prophets wrote about Him
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Jesus asks, “…have you not read what God said to you…” (Matthew 22:31). The words He points to are what God said. He doesn't mention the prophets there.
Nothing about elders here, baker. Jesus asks, “…have you not read what God said to you…” (Matthew 22:31). He sends them straight to what God said. No middleman.

Right, baker. Jesus says, “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” (Matthew 22:32). He says it after quoting God's words about Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. That's the heart of His answer on whether the dead rise.
Good word, friend, but it isn't the one Jesus uses. He says, “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” (Matthew 22:32). The contrast is dead and living. Keep that pair together.

Humble is a fine word, baker, but not what Jesus says here. He says, “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” (Matthew 22:32). The contrast is between the dead and the living. Put those two together and the verse sticks.

That's right, friend. Matthew writes, “When the crowds heard this, they were astonished at His teaching.” (Matthew 22:33). Seven brothers, a tricky question, and Jesus answers it in a few verses. Jaws on the floor, I'd say.

Matthew doesn't say the crowds were offended. He says, “When the crowds heard this, they were astonished at His teaching.” (Matthew 22:33). The Sadducees say there is no resurrection (Matthew 22:23), so Jesus tells them they don't know the Scriptures or the power of God. Then He points to God's own words, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob…” and says, “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” (Matthew 22:32). That's the teaching that left the crowds amazed.

Troubled isn't the word, baker. Matthew says, “When the crowds heard this, they were astonished at His teaching.” (Matthew 22:33). Astonished is more like standing there with your mouth open, forgetting you were holding a cookie. The crowds were amazed at what Jesus taught.
